_comment: CFG-1. The complete, authoritative default. Profiles overlay this; a profile is partial and states only what it changes. The orchestrator reads this file at the start of every run and snapshots the merged result into the workspace.
_comment_tone: CFG-1a. `tone` is null on purpose. It used to say hard-scifi, and because every prompt carries it and all eight agents used to declare themselves hard science fiction in their own files, the genre was effectively welded shut: a cyberpunk premise came back as an engineering document and a premise about a pop star eating quesadillas came back with factions and a bandwidth budget. Null means the orchestrator reads the genre off the premise and writes what it decided into the run's config.snapshot.json, so the choice is recorded rather than assumed. Set it here or in the form to override.
_comment_names: CFG-1b. `familiar` asks for names a reader can pronounce on sight and tell apart in a glance. A run set in north Java produced Nayla Wiryawan, Ilham Basri, Oskar Maas, Ratri Sundoro and Juno Halim inside fourteen hundred words, which is a cast list a reader cannot hold. Set it to `setting` to let the world choose instead, or write any instruction you like: it is passed to the character architect verbatim.
_comment_bible: CFG-2a. These counts are the SIZE OF THE BOOK'S CANON and every profile now overrides them. They used to be inherited unchanged by all four profiles, so a three-chapter run of fourteen hundred words was handed the same four factions, six technologies, eight rules, seven characters, twelve timeline rows and five mysteries as a twelve-chapter novel — and spent every chapter introducing canon it had no room to use. That is what an incoherent short run is made of.
_comment_context: The bounded-context policy. forbid_prior_chapter_prose is no longer a runtime assertion over an assembled prompt: the chapter-writer subagent has its own context window and a tool list of Glob alone, which returns paths and cannot return file contents. The flag stays because it is the thing the architecture is for, and because a future orchestrator that widened the tool list should be failing a stated rule rather than quietly changing one.
_comment_gate: LOOP-003. FIVE characteristics, aggregated with min, so a chapter is only as good as its worst. length and chatter are arithmetic the orchestrator runs in the shell and they reproduce; continuity, science and outline are subagents and they do not. max_revisions counts rewrites, so 2 allows the three attempts LOOP-003 specifies.
_comment_gate_outline: `outline` is the fifth, added by LOOP-003 because nothing checked that the writer wrote the chapter the outline commissioned. Continuity checks the draft against the Bible, science against the world's rules, length and chatter are arithmetic — between them a chapter that is consistent, correctly sized and about something else entirely passed. It scores 10 minus 3 per missing beat minus 1 per beat out of order.
_comment_gate_on_fail: `patch_then_halt` replaces `accept_with_warnings`, which was the exit LOOP-003 G1 exists to close: a chapter that failed three times went into the book with a note in the margin. Now the orchestrator applies the critics' own literal replacements and rescores. If it still fails, the RUN STOPS — by construction that means a critic's replacement was itself wrong and arbitration did not catch it, and that is worth a person's attention before another chapter is written.
_comment_loop003: The feedback that escalates. Each failed attempt must make the next EASIER, not merely better informed: attempt 2 gets a description of the correction, attempt 3 gets the literal sentence. `keep_attempt_drafts` is not optional bookkeeping — without the rejected drafts on disk there is no diff, and LOOP-003 G3 (the writer touches only what was cited) has no instrument at all.
_comment_style: The style pass may not change a word. The orchestrator compares word counts before and after and discards a pass that moved one, so this tolerance is 0 by intent, not by oversight.
_comment_models: Which model each agent runs on is declared in its own .claude/agents/<name>.md front matter, not here. Putting it in two places is how the two disagree.
_comment_models_orchestrator: SPEC-011 W2. The model claude -p runs the ORCHESTRATOR on, passed as --model when set; null means the CLI's own default. The agents' models are in .claude/agents/*.md (all haiku since SPEC-011) and are not this key. Putting the orchestrator on Haiku is a separate decision with a named risk (SPEC-011 §4): the orchestrator arbitrates findings and applies patches. Profiles may override.
_comment_budget: Enforced, measured on the stream (SPEC-007 FR-BUD-1/4, PLAN-007 6.5): the profile's max_cost_usd is passed to claude -p as --max-budget-usd and watched by the backend; the call that crosses it is the last one. NOVAFORGE_BUDGET can only lower it. tiny was 5.0 against a measured $18.82 and is 25.0 since PLAN-007 (P-1, approved with the plan). max_calls is still advisory.
_comment_context_v2: ANNEX B / D13. max_concurrent_tokens is the capacity of the token semaphore in commons/context, and it is CONCURRENT: the sum of every model call in flight at one instant. Not per call - five critics of 30,000 satisfy a per-call limit and put 150,000 in the air. A call reserves prompt tokens (counted, never estimated) plus max_tokens, waits if capacity is short, and releases when it finishes. A reservation larger than this number is halted: context, not an infinite wait.
_comment_summary_facts: The rolling summary is a list of structured facts, capped by COUNT rather than by words, because a count is countable and a word cap was not. When it bites, every open-question survives first, then recent state-change, then event; dropping an open-question warns at run level and does not halt.
